plants.summary: Fine-textured shrub with small fragrant white-pink flowers from early summer to fall, busy with bees and butterflies.
designNotes: Compact and variegated cultivars stay under 1 m.
Thin old stems in late winter rather than shearing.

plants.nativeRange: Mountains of the western U.S., including Arizona and New Mexico
plants.summary: Soft blue-green fir that tolerates heat, drought and alkaline soil better than other firs. A softer-looking alternative to blue spruce.
designNotes: Needs good drainage; root rot in heavy wet clay.
Suited to the Northeast and the Southwest mountains, not the low desert.

plants.summary: Refined small tree with lobed leaves and layered branching; hundreds of cultivars range from dwarf weeping forms to small upright trees, in green, red and variegated leaf.
designNotes: Afternoon shade prevents leaf scorch in hot regions; it struggles in low-desert heat.
Cultivar size varies tenfold — always record the cultivar.
Seeds into woodlands in parts of the Northeast; prefer non-fruiting or dwarf forms near natural areas.

plants.summary: Dense, shade-casting European maple once planted widely as a street tree. It seeds heavily into woodlands, where its shade suppresses native understory.
designNotes: Shallow roots and deep shade make lawn and beds beneath nearly impossible.
Substitute red maple, sugar maple, black gum or a native oak.

plants.summary: Adaptable native shade tree that tolerates wet and compacted soils. Small red flowers open before the leaves and fall colour ranges from yellow to scarlet depending on the seed source or cultivar.
designNotes: Shallow surface roots lift paving and compete with lawn; keep at least 2 m from walks and drives.
Leaves yellow (iron chlorosis) on alkaline soils — avoid where pH is above about 7.5.
Named cultivars give predictable fall colour; for wildlife value, local-ecotype seedlings are equally good.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern Canada and the northeastern and central U.S., south in the Appalachians
plants.summary: Long-lived, dense-crowned shade tree and the classic source of orange-red New England fall colour. Best in deep, cool, well-drained soils.
designNotes: Sensitive to road salt, soil compaction and reflected heat; a poor street tree in tight urban sites.
In the Southeast use only at higher elevations; it struggles in coastal-plain heat.
Dense shade and shallow roots make lawn beneath difficult — plan shade-tolerant groundcover.

plants.nativeRange: Circumboreal; native forms across North America
plants.summary: Ferny, aromatic perennial with flat flower clusters, tolerant of drought, poor soil and mowing. Coloured cultivars are widely sold.
designNotes: Spreads by rhizomes; can be mown into a drought-tolerant lawn alternative.
Flops in rich, wet soil — cut back after first bloom.

plants.nativeRange: Southeastern U.S., from North Carolina to Florida and Texas, north in the Mississippi valley to Illinois
plants.summary: Large shrub or small understory tree with upright clusters of red tubular flowers in early spring, timed with the return of ruby-throated hummingbirds. Thrives in the dappled shade of larger trees.
designNotes: Often drops its leaves in late summer, especially in sun or drought — site it where early bareness is not a focal point.
Seeds, leaves and bark are poisonous; avoid where children or pets may eat the nuts.

plants.nativeRange: Mountains of Arizona, New Mexico and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Fine-leaved, licorice-scented hyssop with smoky orange tubular flowers in late summer, adored by hummingbirds.
designNotes: Needs lean, fast-draining soil; dies in wet winter clay.
Wait until spring to cut back old stems.

plants.summary: Huge blue-gray rosette of toothed, spine-tipped leaves. After 10–25 years it sends up a tall flower stalk and the main rosette dies, leaving pups.
designNotes: Site at least 1.5 m from walks; terminal spines are dangerous.
Remove pups to keep a single specimen.
Sap can irritate skin.

plants.summary: Small, solitary blue-green agave with red-and-yellow leaf edges that glow when backlit. Modest spines make it suitable near paths.
designNotes: Afternoon shade in the low desert prevents yellowing.
Protect below about −4 °C.

plants.nativeRange: Mountains of Arizona, New Mexico and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Compact, symmetrical gray agave with dark terminal spines, shaped like an artichoke. One of the cold-hardiest agaves.
designNotes: Flowers once after many years, then the rosette dies; offsets continue the clump.
Excellent in containers and rock gardens; needs sharp drainage in wet-winter climates.

plants.summary: Clump-forming aloe with fleshy, gray-green leaves and yellow flower spikes in late winter. Spreads by offsets into colonies.
designNotes: Light afternoon shade in the low desert; leaves redden under stress.
Damaged below about −2 °C.

plants.summary: Four-season small tree: early white flowers, early-summer berries birds strip quickly, orange-red fall colour and smooth gray bark.
designNotes: Native alternative to Callery pear for early white bloom.
Often sold multi-stem; prune basal suckers to keep a tree form.

plants.nativeRange: Atlantic Coastal Plain and Piedmont from eastern Canada to Georgia and Alabama
plants.summary: Upright multi-stemmed serviceberry that forms suckering clumps, with white flowers before the leaves, sweet early-summer berries that birds strip quickly and orange-red fall colour. Tolerates wetter soil than downy serviceberry.
designNotes: Serviceberry species and hybrids are often mislabelled in the trade; buy by habit (multi-stem suckering shrub) as much as by name.
Rust and leaf spot are cosmetic; give air movement.
Remove suckers if a tidy clump is wanted.

plants.summary: Feathery, needle-leaved perennial with pale blue spring stars and outstanding golden fall colour. Shrub-like by its third year.
designNotes: Slow to fill in — space for the mature size.
Cut back to 30 cm after bloom if it flops in part shade.

plants.summary: Delicate woodland-edge perennial with nodding red-and-yellow spurred flowers timed with the return of hummingbirds in spring.
designNotes: Short-lived but reseeds into rocky, well-drained spots.
Leaf miners trace lines in leaves — cosmetic; cut foliage back after bloom.

plants.summary: Tough native shrub with white spring flowers, glossy black fruit and brilliant red fall colour. Tolerates both wet and dry soils.
designNotes: Suckers into colonies; compact cultivars (e.g. 'Low Scape Mound') work as a mass groundcover.
A native substitute for burning bush's red fall colour.

plants.summary: Deciduous woodland groundcover with velvety heart-shaped leaves that overlap into a soft carpet in full shade.
designNotes: Flowers are hidden at ground level.
Spreads slowly by rhizomes; plant closely for faster cover.

plants.summary: Clump-forming milkweed for moist soil, with vanilla-scented pink flowers and narrow leaves. A tidy monarch host for rain gardens.
designNotes: Unlike common milkweed it does not run.
Tolerates average garden soil if not allowed to dry out.

plants.nativeRange: Sonoran and Mojave Deserts of Arizona, Nevada, California and northwestern Mexico
plants.summary: Clump of nearly leafless, rush-like gray-green stems topped with clusters of cream flowers from spring through fall. A low-water host plant for monarch and queen butterflies in desert gardens.
designNotes: Milky sap is toxic and irritating; keep away from play areas.
Oleander aphids are common and do no lasting harm — avoid insecticides on milkweeds.
Damaged by hard frost below about −4 °C; best in the low desert.

plants.nativeRange: Most of the U.S. east of the Rockies and the Southwest
plants.summary: Bright orange milkweed for dry, sunny sites and a monarch butterfly host plant. Long-lived once its deep taproot is established.
designNotes: Emerges late in spring — mark its spot so it is not dug up.
Deep taproot: plant young plugs and do not divide or move.
Aphids are common and do no lasting harm; avoid insecticides on milkweeds.

plants.nativeRange: Garden hybrid of East Asian species
plants.summary: Ferny shade perennial with feathery plumes in pink, red, white or lavender in early summer.
designNotes: Leaves crisp brown in dry soil or afternoon sun.
Leave plumes for winter interest.

plants.summary: Deciduous fern with silver fronds brushed with burgundy along the midribs, brightening dark corners.
designNotes: Colour is best in light shade; dull in deep shade, scorched in sun.
Keep soil evenly moist.

plants.summary: Tough gray native shrub for saline, alkaline and disturbed desert soils. Provides cover and seed for quail and songbirds.
designNotes: Female plants carry papery four-winged seed clusters.
Useful for informal screens and erosion control on dry slopes.

plants.nativeRange: Deserts of the southwestern U.S. and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Woolly silver-leaved desert wildflower with lemon-yellow daisies held above the foliage for much of the year.
designNotes: Short-lived; reseeds into gravel and DG.
Extra water makes it lanky and short-lived.

plants.summary: Long-lived, shrub-sized native perennial with indigo pea flowers in late spring and blue-green foliage all season.
designNotes: Deep-rooted: slow to establish, then very drought-tolerant; do not divide or move.
Flops in shade or rich soil — use a peony ring.

plants.summary: Thorny, deer-proof shrub long used in foundation plantings. It forms dense woodland thickets from bird-sown seed and those thickets support high tick populations.
designNotes: Prohibited in New York and Massachusetts, a noxious weed in Pennsylvania (sale ban enforced from October 2023) and listed invasive in Connecticut, with a state sale ban from October 2028.
Substitute bush honeysuckle (Diervilla), Virginia sweetspire, fragrant sumac 'Gro-Low' or dwarf fothergilla.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern U.S. along rivers and floodplains
plants.summary: Fast multi-stem birch with peeling cinnamon and cream bark. The most heat-tolerant birch and highly resistant to bronze birch borer.
designNotes: Usually sold as a three-stem clump; leave room for the spreading base.
Drops twigs and yellow leaves in summer drought; irrigate or site where soil stays moist.
Chlorotic in alkaline soil.

plants.summary: Vigorous native vine with orange-red trumpet flowers in spring and leaves that turn maroon in winter. Climbs by tendrils with adhesive tips.
designNotes: Prune after spring bloom.
Native alternative to trumpet creeper for walls and large fences.

plants.nativeRange: Garden hybrid of South American species
plants.summary: Thorny, sprawling vine with masses of magenta-red bracts in the heat of the low desert. Covers walls, fences and slopes.
designNotes: Frost burns it back below about −2 °C; it usually regrows from the base.
Blooms best when slightly dry and not overfertilized; sharp thorns.

plants.summary: Fine, low native bunchgrass with eyelash-like seed flags. Used as an unmown meadow or a low-water lawn in the high desert and plains.
designNotes: Warm-season — greens late in spring.
'Blonde Ambition' is a taller ornamental selection.

plants.nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and western Asia
plants.summary: Traditional fine-textured evergreen for formal hedges and parterres. Tolerates shearing and shade.
designNotes: Boxwood blight and box tree moth are spreading; scout regularly and avoid overhead irrigation.
Consider inkberry or Japanese holly where blight is established.
Leaves bronze in exposed winter sun and wind.

plants.summary: Fern-leaved desert shrub with spectacular orange-red flower clusters all summer, at its best in the hottest exposures.
designNotes: Cut to 30–45 cm in late winter; it returns quickly.
Seeds are toxic if eaten; small prickles on stems.

plants.summary: Strictly upright grass with early wheat-coloured plumes. Gives a strong vertical line from June through winter; sterile.
designNotes: Cool-season: cut back in late winter before new growth.
Less effective in hot, humid southern summers.

plants.nativeRange: Deserts of Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, California and Mexico
plants.summary: Fine-textured, low native shrub with powder-puff pink flowers in spring. Fits small spaces and naturalistic desert beds.
designNotes: Deer and rabbits browse it; protect young plants.
Very little water once established.

plants.summary: Loose native shrub grown for clusters of vivid magenta-purple fruit along the stems from late summer into winter, eaten by birds.
designNotes: Cut to 30 cm in late winter for a compact, heavily fruiting plant.
Fruits best in sun; tolerates part shade.

plants.summary: Glossy evergreen shrub that blooms in winter and early spring, in red, pink, white and bicolours. A signature plant of southern shade gardens.
designNotes: Morning sun and afternoon shade; hard freezes brown open flowers and buds.
Tea scale on leaf undersides is the common pest — check annually.

plants.summary: Fall-blooming camellia with smaller leaves and more sun tolerance than Japanese camellia. Makes a flowering evergreen hedge.
designNotes: Prune lightly after flowering in winter.
Flower petals shatter and drop rather than browning on the plant.

plants.summary: Vigorous self-clinging native vine with large orange trumpets all summer. Best on a sturdy, freestanding structure where it can be contained.
designNotes: Aerial roots damage siding and wood; root suckers pop up metres away.
Prune hard in late winter to control size.

plants.summary: Soft, fine-textured native sedge that forms a low, lawn-like mat in dry shade under trees. Can be left unmown or mown high.
designNotes: Plant plugs 20–30 cm apart; fills in over 2–3 years.
Not for foot traffic or wet soil.

plants.nativeRange: Sonoran Desert of Arizona and Sonora
plants.summary: The iconic columnar cactus of the Sonoran Desert, growing extremely slowly to great height. White night-blooming flowers feed bats, birds and bees.
designNotes: Protected by Arizona's native plant law; transplanting needs a permit and tag.
Young saguaros need a nurse plant or shade cloth against summer sun.
Never irrigate heavily — water-logged saguaros rot and topple.

plants.summary: Shade-tolerant small native tree with smooth, sinewy gray bark and orange to red fall colour. Suits woodland edges and narrow side yards.
designNotes: One of few small trees that thrive in shade and periodically wet soil.
Slow to establish; plant container-grown stock.

plants.summary: Compact mounding fountain grass with fuzzy bottlebrush plumes in late summer. Popular for edging and mass plantings.
designNotes: Seeds into nearby beds in some areas; cut plumes before seed ripens if needed.
Different from tender, invasive purple and crimson fountain grasses.

plants.nativeRange: North and East Africa and the Middle East
plants.summary: Showy bunchgrass with pink-tan bottlebrush plumes. In Arizona it spreads from yards into desert washes and carries fire into saguaro communities.
designNotes: Use native deer grass or bull grass instead; sterile purple fountain grass (Cenchrus 'Rubrum') is generally treated differently — check local rules.
Remove existing plants before seed ripens.

plants.nativeRange: Much of North America east of the Rockies, plus riparian Arizona, New Mexico and California
plants.summary: Native wetland shrub with spherical white pincushion flowers in summer that draw butterflies and bees. Thrives in standing water.
designNotes: Leafs out late and can look rangy; cut back hard in late winter to renew.
Best at pond edges, swales and rain-garden bottoms.

plants.summary: Small understory tree whose bare branches turn magenta-pink in early spring, followed by heart-shaped leaves. Good under taller trees and at woodland edges.
designNotes: Relatively short-lived (often 20–30 years); plant young and avoid moving established trees.
Weeping, purple-leaf and gold-leaf cultivars exist — record the cultivar, since sizes differ.

plants.summary: Slow, irregular dwarf conifer with shell-like sprays of glossy dark green foliage. A refined accent near patios and entries.
designNotes: Shelter from drying winter wind; inner foliage browns naturally each fall.
Needs moist, well-drained soil.

plants.summary: Clumping, shrub-scaled fan palm with several short trunks. Suits courtyards and large containers where a full-size palm will not fit.
designNotes: Spiny leaf stalks — prune with gloves and keep back from paths.
Takes brief cold to about −9 °C as well as both desert and humid heat.

plants.summary: Shade-tolerant native grass with flat, oat-like seed heads that dangle and turn bronze in fall.
designNotes: Reseeds freely; deadhead before seed drops in tidy beds.
One of few ornamental grasses for shade.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern North America, from Newfoundland to Georgia and west to Minnesota
plants.summary: Late-season wetland perennial with hooded white flowers, sometimes pink-tinged, that only strong bumble bees can push open. The main host plant of the Baltimore checkerspot butterfly.
designNotes: Best in consistently moist to wet soil; leaves scorch in dry sun.
Pinch stems in early summer for bushier, shorter plants that need no staking.

plants.nativeRange: Desert washes of the southwestern U.S. and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Small, airy desert tree with willow-like leaves and orchid-like trumpet flowers from late spring through summer. Hardy into colder high-desert areas.
designNotes: Seedless cultivars avoid the long, persistent seed pods.
Bare and twiggy in winter; pair with evergreen shrubs.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern U.S. from New Jersey to Florida and Texas
plants.summary: Small native tree covered in fringe-like, lightly fragrant white flowers in late spring. Female plants follow with dark blue fruit for birds.
designNotes: Leafs out late — do not mistake it for dead in spring.
Can be attacked by emerald ash borer; monitor where the borer is present.

plants.nativeRange: Hybrid of desert willow and southern catalpa
plants.summary: Fast hybrid tree with long summer bloom of pale pink trumpet flowers and fuller leaves than desert willow.
designNotes: Prone to powdery mildew and leaf scorch with overhead watering.
Shorter-lived than desert willow; plan replacement.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern U.S., from Pennsylvania south to northern Florida and west to Louisiana
plants.summary: Low native groundcover of hairy dark green leaves with bright yellow star-shaped daisies from early spring into summer, and often again in fall. Fills shady edges and slopes under deciduous trees.
designNotes: Needs some shade in hot climates; tolerates sun only where soil stays moist.
Keep leaf litter light over the crowns so they do not rot.

plants.summary: Classic large-flowered clematis with velvety violet-purple flowers through summer on a trellis, mailbox or shrub.
designNotes: Shade the root zone and keep the top in sun.
Group 3 pruning: cut all stems to 30 cm in late winter.

plants.nativeRange: Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain from Maine to Florida and Texas
plants.summary: Native shrub with spicy-fragrant white flower spikes in midsummer when little else blooms. A top bee and butterfly plant for wet, acidic sites.
designNotes: Leafs out late in spring.
Suckers into small colonies; compact cultivars (e.g. 'Hummingbird', 'Sixteen Candles') stay under 1 m.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern U.S., from New Jersey and Pennsylvania west to Kansas and south to Florida and Texas
plants.summary: Late-season native with fluffy powder-blue flower heads like a perennial ageratum, crowded with butterflies and bees from late summer to frost. Spreads by rhizomes into loose drifts in moist soil.
designNotes: Runs freely in rich moist beds — give it room or edge it; it is easy to pull.
Cut back by half in early summer to keep it from flopping.

plants.summary: Cheerful yellow daisy for poor, sandy, sunny soils; reseeds to form colonies along roadsides and meadows.
designNotes: Deadhead for longer bloom, or leave seed for finches and new plants.
Short-lived in rich, wet soil.

plants.summary: Fine, needle-leaved coreopsis with pale butter-yellow flowers from early summer into fall. Blends with blues and purples.
designNotes: Shear by a third after the first flush for more bloom.
Can be short-lived in wet winter soils; give drainage.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern North America, south in the Appalachians to Georgia and Alabama
plants.summary: Small understory tree with distinctive horizontal, tiered branches, flat clusters of creamy flowers in late spring and blue-black fruit on red stalks that birds take in midsummer. Best in cool, moist, partly shaded sites.
designNotes: Heat and drought stress invite golden canker, which kills branches; avoid hot, exposed sites and keep the root zone mulched.
In the Southeast use only at mountain elevations.

plants.summary: Layered native understory tree with white spring bracts, red fruit for migrating birds and red-purple fall colour.
designNotes: Dogwood anthracnose is worst in shady, humid, stagnant sites; give morning sun and air movement.
Mulch the root zone and keep mowers and string trimmers off the thin bark.
Shallow roots dislike drought — irrigate the first two summers.

plants.nativeRange: Northern and western North America, south in the mountains to Arizona and New Mexico
plants.summary: Multi-stemmed native shrub grown for bright red winter stems. Thrives in wet soils and stabilizes stream banks.
designNotes: Stem colour is brightest on young wood — remove a third of the oldest stems each late winter.
Leaf spot and canker are common in hot, humid summers; it is best in the North.

plants.summary: Fast, soft-textured conifer with reddish shredding bark. A reliable large screen for the upper South and mild Northeast.
designNotes: Foliage bronzes in cold winters and greens again in spring.
Better disease record in the Southeast than Leyland cypress.

plants.nativeRange: Mountains of Arizona, New Mexico, west Texas and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Silver-blue, heat- and drought-tolerant cypress for screens and windbreaks. Selections such as 'Carolina Sapphire' are also grown in the Southeast.
designNotes: Needs sharp drainage; root rot in heavy, irrigated clay.
Fairly short-lived in humid climates.

plants.nativeRange: Chihuahuan Desert of Texas and Mexico
plants.summary: Silver-gray, mounding desert groundcover with small purple flower clusters in spring. Spreads across hot slopes and medians.
designNotes: Needs fast drainage; overwatering causes root rot.
Freeze damage below about −7 °C; cut back damaged growth in spring.

plants.nativeRange: Arizona, New Mexico, west Texas and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Dense, spherical rosette of narrow blue-gray leaves edged with hooked teeth. Forms a short trunk with age.
designNotes: Leaf teeth snag skin and clothing — keep 1 m from paths.
Flower stalks reach 3–5 m but the plant does not die after flowering.

plants.summary: Succulent mat covered in glistening magenta daisies all summer. Thrives in hot, dry gravel and rock gardens.
designNotes: Winter-wet soil kills it faster than cold.
Not for foot traffic.

plants.nativeRange: Texas, southern New Mexico and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Slow evergreen shrub or small tree with glossy leaflets and grape-scented violet flower clusters in early spring.
designNotes: Seeds are highly toxic; avoid where children play.
Genista caterpillars can defoliate it in spring — usually recovers.

plants.nativeRange: Northeastern North America and the Great Lakes
plants.summary: Small suckering native shrub with yellow summer flowers and bronze fall colour. Handles dry shade and banks; a native substitute for barberry in low hedges.
designNotes: Not related to invasive Asian bush honeysuckles.
Cut back in late winter to keep it dense.

plants.nativeRange: Pantropical; native in Arizona and Florida
plants.summary: Fast, upright evergreen for informal screens in hot, dry sites. Purple-leaved forms add colour; papery seed capsules follow the inconspicuous flowers.
designNotes: Tolerates shearing as a formal hedge.
Frost damage is possible below about −7 °C.

plants.summary: Long-blooming prairie perennial with drooping rose-purple petals around a bronze cone. Seedheads feed goldfinches into winter.
designNotes: Leave seedheads standing over winter; cut back in late winter.
Many novelty-colour hybrids are shorter-lived than the species; aster yellows disease distorts flowers — remove affected plants.

plants.summary: Clumping small cactus with colourful spines and large magenta flowers in spring. Suits rock gardens and containers.
designNotes: Rots with summer overwatering; plant in gravelly mounds.
Fruit is eaten by birds.

plants.nativeRange: Southern Europe and western to central Asia
plants.summary: Silver-leaved, thorny tree once used for windbreaks. It spreads along western rivers and ditches, crowding out native cottonwoods and willows.
designNotes: Do not plant near streams, ditches or wetlands.
In New Mexico consider New Mexico olive (Forestiera pubescens) or desert willow instead.

plants.summary: Silver-leaved desert shrub that covers itself in bright yellow daisies in late winter and spring. Quick to fill new desert plantings.
designNotes: Short-lived but reseeds; cut back lightly after bloom.
Overwatering makes it floppy and green-leaved.

plants.nativeRange: California, Arizona, New Mexico and the Intermountain West
plants.summary: Low, gray-leaved perennial covered in scarlet tubular flowers in late summer and fall, feeding migrating hummingbirds.
designNotes: Spreads by rhizomes in loose soil.
Cut back hard in winter.

plants.nativeRange: Arid and semi-arid western North America, from southern Canada to northern Mexico
plants.summary: Gray-green, broom-like native shrub that turns into a mound of golden-yellow flowers in early fall, when it is one of the main nectar sources for late butterflies and bees in the high desert.
designNotes: Cut back hard in late winter every few years to keep it dense.
Most at home in high desert and plateau gardens; in the low desert it needs a little summer water and afternoon relief.

plants.summary: Popular hedge shrub prized for intense red fall colour. Birds spread its seed, and shade-tolerant seedlings carpet northeastern forest understories.
designNotes: "Compact" cultivars still seed and still reach 2–3 m.
For red fall colour use black chokeberry, highbush blueberry, fothergilla or Virginia sweetspire.

plants.nativeRange: Atlantic Coastal Plain from Nova Scotia to South Carolina (species)
plants.summary: Compact Joe-Pye weed with domed mauve flower heads that swarm with butterflies in late summer. Sized for home rain gardens.
designNotes: Wilts in drought; best in consistently moist soil.
Leave stems for winter structure and overwintering insects.

plants.nativeRange: Northern U.S. and southern Canada, south in the Appalachians to North Carolina and Tennessee
plants.summary: Tall wetland perennial with purple-spotted stems and broad, flat-topped mauve flower heads that draw swallowtails and bees in late summer. Gives height to the back of rain gardens and wet meadows.
designNotes: Cut stems back by about a third in early June for shorter, sturdier plants.
Wilts quickly in drought; best where soil stays moist all summer.
For small gardens use the compact Little Joe (Eutrochium dubium) instead.

plants.summary: Native shrub with white rose-like flowers followed by feathery pink seed plumes that glow in low sun. Hardy from high to low desert.
designNotes: Suckers modestly — useful on dry slopes.
Very little water once established; overwatering shortens its life.

plants.nativeRange: Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts of Arizona, New Mexico, Texas and Mexico
plants.summary: Large native barrel cactus with hooked spines and a crown of orange to yellow flowers in summer, followed by yellow fruit eaten by wildlife.
designNotes: Barrels lean south with age; plant with the original south face oriented south.
Keep well away from walks and play areas.

plants.summary: Vigorous arching shrub whose bare stems turn bright yellow in early spring. Fast screen for banks and property edges.
designNotes: Avoid shearing into boxes — remove the oldest canes at the base after bloom.
Flower buds can be killed in zone 4–5 winters; hardier cultivars exist.

plants.nativeRange: Coastal Plain of the Carolinas, Georgia, Florida and Alabama
plants.summary: Compact native shrub with honey-scented white bottlebrush flowers in spring and some of the best orange-red-yellow fall colour of any shrub.
designNotes: Needs acidic, well-drained soil.
Fall colour is best in full sun.

plants.summary: Cluster of tall, spiny, unbranched canes that leaf out after each rain and carry red flower tips in spring. A living sculpture or fence.
designNotes: Bare-root transplants can take a year to leaf out; leafing confirms establishment, not death.
Protected under Arizona's native plant law: buy tagged nursery or salvage plants.

plants.nativeRange: Southern and central U.S. to northern Mexico, including Florida and Gulf Coast dunes and the Southwest; naturalized northward along the Atlantic coast
plants.summary: Annual or short-lived perennial daisy with red petals tipped in yellow around a dark centre, blooming from spring to frost. Thrives on hot sand and salt spray where few flowers will.
designNotes: Behaves as a reseeding annual; leave some seedheads and bare sandy soil for new plants.
Rich soil and irrigation make it floppy and short-lived.
Perennial blanket flower hybrids (Gaillardia × grandiflora) are a different plant.

plants.summary: Glossy evergreen shrub with intensely fragrant white flowers in late spring. Best near patios and windows where the scent carries.
designNotes: Needs acidic soil; yellow leaves on alkaline soil signal iron deficiency.
Whiteflies and sooty mould are common; hardier cultivars extend it into zone 7.

plants.nativeRange: Southeastern U.S. from Virginia to Florida and Texas
plants.summary: Fine-textured native evergreen vine covered in fragrant yellow trumpets in late winter and early spring. Covers fences and arbors.
designNotes: All parts are toxic if eaten.
Prune right after flowering; cut back hard if the top gets heavy and bare below.

plants.summary: Sprawling hardy geranium with violet-blue, white-eyed flowers from early summer to frost. Weaves through neighbours and covers ground.
designNotes: Trim back by half in midsummer if it gets leggy.
Afternoon shade in hot climates.

plants.summary: Male ginkgo selection with fan-shaped leaves that turn butter-yellow and drop almost all at once in fall. Exceptionally tolerant of urban stress.
designNotes: Male clone — avoids the foul-smelling fruit of female trees.
Slow and gangly when young; fills out after 10–15 years.

plants.summary: Low, sprawling native verbena with clusters of magenta to pink flowers from spring to frost. Spills over walls and fills hot, dry edges.
designNotes: Short-lived in heavy wet soils; needs sharp drainage.
'Homestead Purple' is a widely sold selection.

plants.summary: Thornless, largely seedless honeylocust with a broad pyramidal crown. Fine leaflets cast light, filtered shade that lets lawn and perennials grow beneath.
designNotes: Tiny leaflets drop and disappear into lawns — little raking.
Widely planted; mix with other species to avoid monoculture pest outbreaks (plant bug, webworm).

plants.summary: Cascading gold-and-green grass that lights up shade, with leaves that all sweep in one direction.
designNotes: Slow to establish; plant generously.
Scorches in hot afternoon sun.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern North America, from Nova Scotia to Florida and west to Texas and Minnesota
plants.summary: Large native shrub or small multi-stemmed tree with spidery, lightly fragrant yellow flowers in October and November, often as the gold fall leaves drop. Grows in sun or the shade of a woodland edge.
designNotes: Not the late-winter hybrid witch hazels (Hamamelis × intermedia), which bloom in February–March.
Remove root suckers to keep a tree form, or let it thicket as an informal screen.
Flowers best with a few hours of direct sun.

plants.nativeRange: Florida, the Caribbean and tropical America
plants.summary: Fast native shrub with tubular red-orange flowers from late spring to frost, heavily used by hummingbirds and butterflies.
designNotes: Freezes to the ground in zone 9 and often resprouts; cut back in late winter.
Native alternative to lantana in Florida.

plants.summary: Compact reblooming daylily with golden-yellow flowers from early summer to fall. A durable edging and commercial mass planting.
designNotes: Deer eat daylily buds — avoid where browsing is heavy.
Remove spent scapes for a tidier look; divide every 4–5 years.

plants.nativeRange: Central and west Texas and northeastern Mexico
plants.summary: Grass-like clump of arching leaves with spineless tips and tall coral flower stalks from spring through fall. Not a true yucca.
designNotes: Safe near walks — no sharp spines.
Deer and rabbits eat flower stalks.

plants.summary: Native foliage perennial with mottled, often silvery leaves and airy cream flower stalks. Tolerates dry shade under trees.
designNotes: Parent of many coloured-leaf hybrids; the species is longer-lived in heat and humidity.
Replant crowns that heave out of the ground after frost.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern and central U.S., from Massachusetts and the Great Lakes to Florida and Texas
plants.summary: Shrub-sized native perennial for wet ground, with dinner-plate white or pink flowers, usually with a crimson eye, through late summer. Dies to the ground each winter and regrows quickly.
designNotes: Emerges very late in spring — mark its position so it is not dug up or planted over.
Hibiscus sawfly larvae skeletonise leaves in some years; plants recover.
Wild plants range from white to pink; many large-flowered hybrids are sold under this name.

plants.summary: Upright shrub with large hibiscus flowers from midsummer to early fall, when few shrubs bloom. White, pink, purple and blue cultivars.
designNotes: Seeds prolifically into beds; specify sterile or low-seed cultivars.
Leafs out very late in spring.

plants.summary: Huge chartreuse-gold hosta with thick, slug-resistant leaves that brighten shade. A bold specimen or edge for woodland beds.
designNotes: Gold colour needs some morning sun; afternoon sun scorches it.
Deer browse hostas heavily.

plants.summary: Self-clinging woody vine for shaded walls, with lacecap white flowers in early summer and peeling cinnamon bark in winter.
designNotes: Slow for 2–3 years before it climbs; then very vigorous.
Needs a sturdy masonry wall or large tree trunk.

plants.summary: Reliable native hydrangea with huge rounded white flower heads in early summer, aging to green. Blooms on new wood, so it flowers even after a hard winter.
designNotes: Cut stems to 15–30 cm in late winter; strong-stemmed selections flop less after rain.
Wilts in afternoon sun and drought — best with morning sun and moist soil.

plants.summary: Classic mophead and lacecap hydrangea of coastal gardens. Flower colour shifts blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil.
designNotes: Flower buds form the previous summer; late frosts and fall pruning remove the bloom. Reblooming series flower on new wood too.
Wilts daily in afternoon sun — morning sun and steady moisture.

plants.summary: Large panicle hydrangea with lime-tinted flower heads that age to cream and pink. The most sun-tolerant and dependable hydrangea for cold climates.
designNotes: Blooms on new wood — cut back by a third in late winter.
For small spaces, 'Little Lime' reaches about 1–1.5 m.
Can be trained as a small standard tree.

plants.summary: Bold native shrub with large oak-shaped leaves, cone-shaped white panicles that age pink, burgundy fall colour and peeling winter bark.
designNotes: Flowers on old wood — shape only right after bloom.
Needs good drainage; root rot in heavy, wet clay.
Compact cultivars (e.g. 'Ruby Slippers', 'Pee Wee') fit foundations.

plants.summary: Succulent-leaved perennial with broccoli-like heads that open pink in late summer and age to rust, standing through winter.
designNotes: Splays open in rich soil or shade; pinch back by half in early summer.
Leave dried heads for winter interest.

plants.summary: Small-leaved evergreen holly widely used for clipped hedges and foundation shapes. Columnar forms such as 'Sky Pencil' fit narrow spaces.
designNotes: Black root rot and spider mites appear in poorly drained or hot, dry sites.
Bird-sown seedlings escape into woodlands in parts of the mid-Atlantic; inkberry is the native alternative.

plants.nativeRange: Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain from Nova Scotia to Florida and Louisiana
plants.summary: Native evergreen holly with small spineless leaves, used as a boxwood substitute for hedges and foundations. Tolerates wet, acidic soils.
designNotes: The species becomes open at the base with age; compact cultivars (e.g. 'Shamrock', 'Gem Box') stay dense.
Suckers to form colonies — useful for massing, a nuisance in tight beds.

plants.summary: Fast, dense, glossy hybrid holly that fruits heavily without a pollinator. A standard tall privacy screen in the upper South.
designNotes: Grows wide; space at least 2 m apart and keep 1.5 m from walks.
Tea scale can build up on stressed plants.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern U.S. from Massachusetts to Florida and Texas
plants.summary: Native evergreen holly with spiny matte leaves and red winter berries on female trees. A dense pyramidal screen that tolerates coastal conditions.
designNotes: Plants are male or female: specify female cultivars for berries and include a male within about 30 m.
Avoid poorly drained and alkaline soils.

plants.summary: Deciduous native holly whose bare stems are covered in red fruit through early winter. Excellent for wet soils and bird gardens.
designNotes: Only female plants fruit; include one compatible male (early- or late-blooming to match) per 5–10 females within about 15 m.
Chlorotic in alkaline soil.

plants.nativeRange: Southeastern U.S. from Virginia to Florida and Texas
plants.summary: Tough native evergreen holly that tolerates salt, drought, wet soil and shearing. Grows into a large screen or small multi-stem tree.
designNotes: Dwarf forms ('Nana', 'Schillings') stay near 1 m for low hedges.
Female plants bear red fruit; weeping forms make narrow specimens.

plants.summary: Grassy-leaved iris with elegant blue-violet flowers in late spring; foliage stays upright and clean all season.
designNotes: Divide when clumps hollow in the centre.
More disease- and borer-resistant than bearded iris.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern Canada and the northeastern U.S., south to Virginia and west to the Great Lakes
plants.summary: Native wetland iris with sword-like blue-green leaves and violet-blue flowers veined white and yellow in late spring. Grows in saturated soil and shallow standing water, making it a natural choice for rain-garden bottoms and pond edges.
designNotes: Tolerates up to about 10 cm of standing water; in ordinary beds keep it consistently moist.
Rhizomes and sap are mildly toxic and can irritate skin — wear gloves when dividing.
Do not substitute yellow flag (Iris pseudacorus), an invasive wetland iris.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern U.S. from New Jersey to Florida and Texas
plants.summary: Arching native shrub with drooping white flower tassels in late spring and long-lasting red to purple fall colour. Tolerates wet soils and some shade.
designNotes: Spreads by suckers into a thicket — good for slopes and rain gardens, edge it in formal beds.
'Henry's Garnet' and dwarf 'Little Henry' are common selections.

plants.nativeRange: Wetlands of eastern North America (the species is nearly worldwide)
plants.summary: Clumps of smooth, upright, dark green round stems that stay green most of the winter in the South. Tolerates standing water and binds wet soil in rain-garden bottoms, swales and pond edges.
designNotes: Will not tolerate dry beds; plant only where soil stays moist or wet.
Reseeds into bare wet soil; cut out old brown stems in late winter.

plants.summary: Arching, vase-shaped juniper with soft dark green foliage that holds colour in winter. Fills hot, dry banks and large foundation beds.
designNotes: Needs full sun and good drainage; thins and gets blight in shade or wet soil.
Plan for the full spread — shearing leaves bare brown patches.

plants.nativeRange: Northern North America, including northern New England and New York (species)
plants.summary: Flat, silver-blue juniper that spreads into a carpet on sunny slopes. Turns plum-tinged in winter.
designNotes: Weeds are hard to remove once mats close — clear perennial weeds first.
Phomopsis blight hits shaded, wet or overhead-watered plantings.

plants.summary: Tough native juniper for dry, poor and alkaline soils. Female trees bear blue berry-like cones that feed winter birds.
designNotes: Alternate host of cedar-apple rust; keep away from apples and susceptible crabapples.
Narrow cultivars suit tight screens; species seedlings vary in form.

plants.nativeRange: Sonoran Desert of Arizona, California and Mexico
plants.summary: Nearly leafless green-stemmed shrub covered in tubular red flowers in late winter and spring — a key early nectar source for hummingbirds.
designNotes: Drops leaves in drought; stems stay green.
Freeze-damaged tips recover; prune after bloom.

plants.summary: Native broadleaf evergreen with clusters of intricate cup-shaped pink-to-white flowers in late spring. Suits woodland gardens with acidic soil.
designNotes: Leaves are toxic to people, pets and livestock if eaten.
Requires excellent drainage; dislikes heavy clay and alkaline soil.
Many compact and deeply coloured cultivars exist.

plants.summary: Globe-shaped cactus covered in bright golden spines that glow when backlit. Effective massed in gravel beds and containers.
designNotes: Light afternoon shade in the low desert prevents sunburn on young plants.
Nearly extinct in the wild — buy nursery-propagated plants.

plants.summary: Southern summer-flowering small tree with long bloom in white, pink, red or lavender and smooth, mottled bark. Many popular selections are L. indica × L. fauriei hybrids.
designNotes: Choose a cultivar whose mature height fits the space instead of topping ("crape murder"), which causes weak knuckled growth.
Mildew-resistant hybrids are the better choice in humid regions.
Crapemyrtle bark scale is spreading — inspect bark for white felty patches and black sooty mold.

plants.summary: Heat-loving shrub with multicoloured flower clusters, widely sold as a butterfly plant. Its bird-dispersed fruit invades natural areas in Florida and hybridizes with native lantanas.
designNotes: Listed as a Category I invasive in Florida (as Lantana strigocamara, the hybrid complex sold as L. camara); use firebush (Hamelia patens) there.
Unripe berries and leaves are toxic to people, pets and livestock.
In the Southwest it is a common, low-water summer bloomer; cut back in late winter.

plants.summary: Fast, sprawling groundcover with lavender flower clusters for most of the year in hot, dry exposures.
designNotes: Frost burns the tops; cut back in late winter.
Leaves and fruit are toxic to pets and livestock.

plants.summary: Signature shrub of the warm deserts, with resinous olive leaves whose scent fills the air after rain. Needs no irrigation once established.
designNotes: Extra water makes it dense and green; withholding water keeps it open and sculptural.
Thin rather than shear.

plants.summary: Silvery evergreen subshrub with fragrant lavender spikes in early summer. Selected for tolerance of both cold winters and humid summers.
designNotes: Needs sharp drainage and lean soil; root rot in wet clay.
Cut back by a third after bloom, never into bare old wood.

plants.nativeRange: Chihuahuan Desert of Texas and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Silver-leaved desert shrub that flushes with lavender-pink flowers after summer rains. A low-water staple of southwestern landscapes.
designNotes: Shearing into balls removes the flowers — prune selectively in spring.
Overwatering and poor drainage cause leggy, short-lived plants.

plants.summary: Upright spikes of fuzzy purple flowers that open from the top down. Strong vertical accent and butterfly plant.
designNotes: Grows from corms; voles may eat them.
Tolerates wet winters better than most prairie liatris.

plants.summary: Shade-tolerant native shrub with tiny yellow flowers in earliest spring, aromatic leaves, red fruit on female plants and clear yellow fall colour.
designNotes: Host plant of the spicebush swallowtail butterfly.
Male and female plants; plant several for fruit.

plants.nativeRange: Southeastern U.S., north to southern New York and Connecticut
plants.summary: Star-leaved shade tree with long-lasting mixed purple, red and gold fall colour. Spiny seed balls are its main drawback.
designNotes: Keep fruiting forms away from patios, walks and lawns; 'Rotundiloba' is a largely fruitless cultivar.
Surface roots are common in shallow or compacted soils.

plants.summary: One of the tallest eastern hardwoods, with a straight trunk, tulip-shaped flowers high in the crown and clear yellow fall colour.
designNotes: Needs space — too large for most small lots and brittle in ice storms.
Drops yellow leaves early in summer drought.

plants.summary: Clumping, grass-like evergreen with lavender flower spikes in late summer. Standard edging and mass groundcover in the South.
designNotes: Mow or cut back in late winter before new leaves emerge.
Creeping lilyturf (L. spicata) spreads aggressively — specify L. muscari for edging.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern North America and riparian areas of the Southwest
plants.summary: Brilliant scarlet flower spikes for wet soil and stream edges; one of the strongest hummingbird attractants.
designNotes: Short-lived; allow some seedlings to replace parents.
Do not mulch over the basal rosettes in winter.

plants.summary: Well-behaved native twining honeysuckle with coral-red tubular flowers from spring into summer — a key hummingbird vine.
designNotes: Not invasive like Japanese honeysuckle; flowers are unscented.
Aphids and powdery mildew in shade; give sun and air.
Prune lightly after the main spring bloom.

plants.summary: Purple-leaved evergreen shrub with fringe-like pink flowers in spring. A staple of southeastern foundation plantings.
designNotes: Many "dwarf" cultivars outgrow their labels; pick by mature size rather than shearing.
Yellowing in alkaline soil.

plants.nativeRange: Southeastern Coastal Plain from North Carolina to Florida and east Texas
plants.summary: Large evergreen tree with glossy leathery leaves and big fragrant white flowers in late spring. A bold year-round screen where there is room.
designNotes: Dense shade and constant leaf litter make underplanting and lawn nearly impossible; leave lower limbs to the ground.
Compact cultivars (e.g. 'Little Gem') suit small lots; 'Bracken's Brown Beauty' is hardier for zone 6 sites.

plants.nativeRange: Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain from Massachusetts to Florida and Texas
plants.summary: Small multi-stem magnolia for wet, acidic soils, with lemony-fragrant flowers through early summer and silvery leaf undersides that flash in wind.
designNotes: Evergreen in the South, deciduous to semi-evergreen in the North.
Excellent for rain gardens and poorly drained corners where other small trees fail.

plants.summary: Small rounded crabapple with deep pink flowers, reddish-purple new leaves and small persistent dark red fruit that birds take through winter.
designNotes: Chosen for good apple scab resistance; older crabapple cultivars often defoliate by midsummer.
Keep away from eastern red cedar where cedar-apple rust is common.

plants.summary: Small mounding native with honey-scented white daisies nearly year-round in the desert. Thrives in reflected heat and gravel.
designNotes: Overwatering and rich soil kill it — no amendments.
Shear lightly in late winter.

plants.summary: Fine, white-edged leaves give this maiden grass a silvery shimmer. It flowers late and sparsely in cool climates.
designNotes: The species self-seeds into fields and forest edges in parts of the East; cultivars vary in seed set — avoid near natural areas.
Divide old clumps that die out in the centre.

plants.summary: Aromatic native mint with shaggy scarlet flower heads that are among the best hummingbird flowers of the Northeast.
designNotes: Powdery mildew is common in dry soil and still air; mildew-resistant cultivars such as 'Jacob Cline' help.
Spreads by runners — divide every 2–3 years.

plants.summary: Drought-tolerant native bee balm with lavender pompom flowers and oregano-scented leaves. One of the best native bee plants.
designNotes: Lower leaves get mildew by late summer; plant mid-border behind shorter plants.
Seeds in readily in meadows.

plants.nativeRange: Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain from New Jersey to Florida and Texas
plants.summary: Fast native evergreen with aromatic leaves and waxy gray fruit for winter birds. Builds a quick informal screen on coastal and wet sites.
designNotes: Multi-trunked and can splay or split in ice; remove suckers to keep a tree form.
Shorter-lived than hollies — expect 20–30 years.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern and southern U.S., from Massachusetts to Florida and Texas
plants.summary: Fine-textured native grass that erupts into clouds of pink flowers in fall. Spectacular in masses, backlit by low sun.
designNotes: Comb out or cut back old growth in late winter.
Unreliable bloom north of zone 7; very reliable in the South and low desert.

plants.nativeRange: California, Arizona, New Mexico, Texas and Mexico
plants.summary: Large, fine-textured native bunchgrass with upright flower spikes. The go-to replacement for invasive fountain grass in desert landscapes.
designNotes: Cut back to 15–20 cm every few years in late winter to renew.
Good in swales and basins that receive runoff.

plants.summary: Flat, bright green carpet with tiny white star flowers, covering large areas quickly in the low desert.
designNotes: Frost-sensitive below about −4 °C.
Shorter-lived with frequent irrigation; replant thin patches.

plants.summary: Cane-forming evergreen shrub with lacy leaves and red winter berries. Its bird-dispersed seedlings invade southeastern forests, and the berries are toxic to birds and pets.
designNotes: Listed as a Category I invasive in Florida and Category 2 in Georgia.
Low-fruiting dwarf selections pose less risk, but native yaupon, wax myrtle or beautyberry are better choices.

plants.nativeRange: New Mexico, west Texas, Mexico and Argentina
plants.summary: Hair-fine grass that ripples in the slightest breeze, turning blond in summer. Native to New Mexico.
designNotes: Reseeds heavily and is invasive outside its native range in some western states; use with care near natural areas.
Comb out dead blades in late winter rather than cutting hard.

plants.summary: Billowing gray-green perennial with lavender-blue flower spikes from late spring into fall. Despite the name it reaches about 75 cm.
designNotes: Shear by half after the first flush for repeat bloom.
Flops open in rich, wet soil.
Deer and rabbits leave it alone.

plants.summary: Heat-, drought- and salt-proof evergreen screen with long summer bloom in white, pink or red. All parts are highly toxic.
designNotes: Keep away from play areas and grazing animals; never burn clippings.
Oleander leaf scorch has killed many old hedges in parts of the Southwest; dwarf cultivars suit small beds.

plants.nativeRange: Arizona, New Mexico, west Texas and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Fountain of long, wiry grass-like leaves from a woody base, with plumes of cream flowers. Softer than agaves and yuccas for planting near paths.
designNotes: Very drought- and cold-tolerant once rooted.
Remove dead inner leaves by hand, not by shearing.

plants.summary: Glossy-leaved native tree with some of the most reliable scarlet fall colour of any species. Small blue fruit feeds migrating birds; flowers are a key bee forage.
designNotes: Deep taproot — plant young container or small B&B trees.
Tolerates wet soils and short flooding, but also performs on drier upland sites.

plants.summary: Wiry, airy perennial with white to pink butterfly-like flowers dancing above the foliage from spring to fall.
designNotes: Deep taproot: tolerates drought, dislikes moving.
Cut back by half in midsummer if floppy.

plants.nativeRange: Sonoran Desert of Arizona, California and Sonora
plants.summary: Very long-lived Sonoran Desert tree with gray-green foliage and pink-lavender spring flowers. A traditional nurse plant that shelters young cacti.
designNotes: Frost-sensitive when young; limited to the low desert.
Spiny branches — keep off walk edges or raise the canopy as it grows.

plants.nativeRange: Deserts of the southwestern U.S. and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Sprawling native prickly pear with large pads, yellow spring flowers and purple fruit (tunas) eaten by wildlife and people.
designNotes: Fine barbed glochids lodge in skin — handle with tongs and thick gloves.
Easily started from pad cuttings.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern U.S., from Massachusetts to Florida
plants.summary: Low, sprawling native cactus of eastern sand dunes and rock outcrops, with silky yellow flowers in early summer. Pads shrivel in winter and plump again in spring.
designNotes: Needs sharp drainage and full sun.
Glochids are irritating — wear gloves.

plants.summary: Upright, ribbed columnar cactus that branches from the base. Planted in rows as a living fence or as vertical accents.
designNotes: Tip damage below about −3 °C; cover tops on freeze nights.
Short white spines along the ribs — less hazardous than most cacti.

plants.nativeRange: Southeastern U.S., from Kentucky to Florida and Louisiana
plants.summary: Native pachysandra with mottled matte leaves and fragrant bottlebrush flowers in early spring. Clumps slowly rather than running.
designNotes: Native alternative to Japanese pachysandra and English ivy.
Old leaves look tattered by spring — mow or clip before new growth.

plants.summary: Glossy evergreen groundcover for deep shade, spreading by runners into a uniform carpet under trees.
designNotes: Spreads into adjacent woodlands; Allegheny spurge or Pennsylvania sedge are native alternatives.
Volutella blight browns patches in crowded, wet beds.

plants.summary: Fast native groundcover for moist shade, with low rosettes of rounded leaves and bright yellow daisies in spring.
designNotes: Spreads quickly by runners and seed; good for large wet areas, too vigorous for small beds.
Flower stalks reach about 45 cm.

plants.summary: Long-lived perennial with large, often fragrant late-spring flowers and handsome foliage through fall. Can outlive the gardener.
designNotes: Set eyes no more than 5 cm deep or it will not bloom.
Needs winter chill; poor in the Deep South and low desert.
Use rings for heavy double flowers.

plants.nativeRange: Most of North America east of the Rockies, plus Arizona and New Mexico (species)
plants.summary: Compact switchgrass whose leaf tips turn red in summer and burgundy by fall, with airy seed panicles. Handles both wet and dry soils.
designNotes: Clump-forming; cut back in late winter.
Taller cultivars ('Northwind', 'Heavy Metal') make tall screens.

plants.nativeRange: Hybrid selection from Sonoran Desert palo verdes
plants.summary: Thornless, upright hybrid palo verde with green bark and a long spring bloom. The most planted palo verde for patios and streets in the low desert.
designNotes: Complex hybrid of several Parkinsonia species; listed at genus level.
Seed set is low, so litter is lighter than blue palo verde.

plants.nativeRange: Sonoran Desert of Arizona, California and northwestern Mexico
plants.summary: Desert wash tree with blue-green bark that photosynthesizes after the tiny leaves drop. Covered in yellow flowers in spring.
designNotes: Water deeply and infrequently; overwatering produces weak, fast growth that breaks in monsoon winds.
Flower and pod litter is heavy — keep away from pools.

plants.nativeRange: Sonoran Desert uplands of Arizona, southeastern California and northwestern Mexico
plants.summary: Slow-growing, long-lived palo verde of rocky desert slopes, with yellow-green bark, tiny leaves and spine-tipped twigs. Pale yellow flowers cover it in mid-spring, a few weeks after blue palo verde.
designNotes: Needs almost no supplemental water once established; overwatering shortens its life.
Dense, spiny branchlets — keep it back from walks and play areas.
A classic nurse tree for young saguaros in the wild.

plants.summary: Adaptable native vine with five-part leaves that turn brilliant scarlet in fall and blue berries for birds. Climbs walls or covers banks.
designNotes: Clings with adhesive pads — fine on masonry, keep off wood siding and gutters.
Five leaflets (poison ivy has three).

plants.summary: Native herbaceous vine with intricate lavender flowers and egg-shaped fruit. Host plant of gulf fritillary and variegated fritillary butterflies.
designNotes: Dies to the ground in winter and reappears late in spring.
Spreads by root suckers — give it room or a contained bed.

plants.summary: Native beardtongue with burgundy-tinted leaves and stems and white tubular flowers in late spring, popular with bumblebees.
designNotes: Leaf colour is best in full sun and cool weather.
Remove spent stalks or let them seed.

plants.summary: Hardy native penstemon with scarlet tubular flowers on arching stems in spring; adapted from the high desert to the low desert.
designNotes: Cut flower stalks to the rosette after bloom.
Plant in lean gravelly soil; rich soil shortens its life.

plants.nativeRange: Sonoran Desert of southern Arizona and Sonora
plants.summary: Spring-blooming desert penstemon with tall wands of rose-pink flowers rising from blue-green rosettes. Fills desert gardens by reseeding.
designNotes: Short-lived (2–3 years); leave seed stalks until seed drops.
Needs fast drainage and no summer overwatering.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern North America, from Quebec south to northern Florida and west to Texas
plants.summary: Low woodland phlox with loose clusters of fragrant lavender-blue flowers in mid-spring, blooming before the tree canopy closes. Creeping stems knit into an informal carpet under deciduous trees.
designNotes: Pair with ferns, sedges or wild ginger to cover the gap after it goes semi-dormant in summer heat.
Deer and rabbits browse it; protect young plants near woods edges.
Shear lightly after bloom to tidy; powdery mildew is less of a problem in shade with good air movement.

plants.summary: Mildew-resistant garden phlox with clusters of small lilac flowers that butterflies favour over showier cultivars.
designNotes: Thin to 4–5 stems per clump in spring for air movement.
Deer browse phlox heavily — protect or site near the house.

plants.summary: Needle-leaved evergreen mat that disappears under pink, lavender or white flowers in spring. Ideal over walls and on dry, sunny banks.
designNotes: Needs sun and drainage; rots in wet shade.
Shear lightly after flowering to keep mats dense.

plants.nativeRange: North Africa and the Middle East (cultivated origin)
plants.summary: Feather palm with gray-green fronds, widely planted in the low desert as large transplanted specimens. Female palms bear dates.
designNotes: Sharp spines at the frond bases — keep away from walks and pools.
Fruit drop is heavy on female palms unless clusters are removed.

plants.summary: Vigorous ninebark with dark purple foliage, pinkish-white flower clusters and peeling winter bark. Adds contrast to green borders.
designNotes: Powdery mildew is common in humid, still sites; give good air movement.
Remove a few of the oldest stems after flowering to keep it full; compact cultivars exist for small beds.

plants.nativeRange: Boreal North America, south to northern New England and New York (species)
plants.summary: Tight, cone-shaped dwarf spruce with dense fine needles. Used as a formal accent in foundations and containers.
designNotes: Spider mites brown the inner foliage in hot, dry, reflected sites.
Prune out any reverted fast-growing shoots.
Winter burn on the south side in exposed sites; screen from winter sun and wind.

plants.nativeRange: Rocky Mountains, including high elevations of Arizona and New Mexico
plants.summary: Stiff, pyramidal spruce with silver-blue needles in the best selections. Thrives in cool, dry mountain climates.
designNotes: Prone to needle cast and Cytospora canker in the humid East; it often declines after 15–20 years there.
Native to the high mountains of the Southwest but not suited to low-desert heat.

plants.summary: One of the few pines that tolerate low-desert heat and alkaline soil. Used for windbreaks and tall evergreen screens in the Southwest.
designNotes: Water deeply and infrequently; shallow-watered trees topple in monsoon winds.
Pine bark beetles attack drought-stressed trees.

plants.nativeRange: Colorado Plateau and mountains of Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Utah
plants.summary: Small, slow, rounded pine of the high desert, producing edible pine nuts. Defines the look of pinyon-juniper country gardens.
designNotes: For high-desert sites (Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Flagstaff), not the low desert.
Bark beetles kill drought-stressed trees; water deeply during prolonged drought.

plants.nativeRange: Mountains of central and southern Europe (species)
plants.summary: Slow, globe-shaped dwarf pine for rock gardens, containers and small foundation beds in cold climates.
designNotes: Snap new candles back by half in late spring to keep it compact.
Pine sawfly larvae feed in colonies in spring — knock off by hand.

plants.nativeRange: Southeastern Coastal Plain from Virginia to east Texas
plants.summary: Fire-adapted southern pine with very long needles. Wind-firm and long-lived, it anchors restoration plantings with native grasses.
designNotes: Spends several years in a grass-like stage while the root system develops before growing upward.
Plant in deep sandy, well-drained soils; it resents heavy wet clay.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern Canada, the northeastern U.S. and the Appalachians
plants.summary: Soft-needled native pine that grows quickly into a tall, layered tree. Widely used for screening, though it loses lower limbs with age.
designNotes: Very sensitive to road salt spray and ozone; keep away from salted roads.
Poor in heavy clay and alkaline soils.
Deer browse young trees heavily.

plants.nativeRange: Southeastern U.S. from southern New Jersey to central Florida and east Texas
plants.summary: The dominant fast-growing pine of the southern Piedmont and Coastal Plain. Tall, open-crowned and a major source of pine straw.
designNotes: Self-prunes lower branches and drops cones; site well away from houses because large pines fail in hurricanes and ice.
Southern pine beetle outbreaks follow drought — keep stressed stands thinned.

plants.summary: Heat- and drought-tolerant shade tree with brilliant orange-red fall colour even in hot climates. A good deciduous patio tree for the Southwest and Southeast.
designNotes: Seedlings are irregular when young; train to a central leader.
Female trees fruit and can self-seed in some areas — specify male selections where available.

plants.summary: Dense evergreen shrub with whorled leathery leaves and orange-blossom-scented spring flowers. Very salt- and drought-tolerant.
designNotes: 'Wheeler's Dwarf' and variegated dwarf forms stay near 1 m.
Afternoon shade in the low desert.

plants.summary: Narrow, upright evergreen with strap-shaped needles, used for tall clipped hedges and screens in warm humid regions.
designNotes: Shears well; untrimmed plants become small trees.
Fruit is toxic to pets.

plants.summary: Evergreen native fern with leathery dark green fronds that persist through winter. Tolerates drier shade than most ferns.
designNotes: Clip old fronds in early spring as fiddleheads rise.
Excellent on shaded slopes and with spring ephemerals.

plants.nativeRange: Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts of Arizona, New Mexico and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Native desert shade tree with a broad, dappled canopy, fragrant catkin flowers and edible-for-wildlife pods. Leafs out late and drops leaves in hard frost.
designNotes: Deep, infrequent watering builds deep, wind-firm roots; shallow lawn watering causes top-heavy trees that blow over.
Thin the canopy lightly before monsoon season instead of heavy lion-tailing.

plants.summary: Vase-shaped ornamental cherry with heavy clusters of double pink flowers in mid-spring. Showy but relatively short-lived.
designNotes: Typically declines after 15–25 years; needs well-drained soil.
Borers and canker are common on stressed trees — avoid wounding the trunk.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern U.S., from Maine south to Florida and west to Michigan and Texas
plants.summary: Minty native perennial whose small white flowers sit on silvery bracts that look frosted all summer. Among the busiest plants in any garden for wasps, bees and small butterflies.
designNotes: Spreads steadily by rhizomes; contain it in small beds or let it fill a meadow edge.
Aromatic leaves make it unattractive to deer and rabbits.

plants.summary: Formerly ubiquitous street tree with early white bloom. Different cultivars cross-pollinate and seed into thorny thickets in fields and woodland edges; listed as a noxious weed in Pennsylvania.
designNotes: Narrow branch angles split in storms after about 15–20 years.
For early white bloom use serviceberry, fringetree or native plums instead.
Existing trees: removal and replacement are commonly encouraged.

plants.summary: A broad, long-lived oak that supports an exceptional number of native insects and acorn-eating wildlife. Slow to establish but extremely durable once rooted.
designNotes: Plant small (container or 1.5–2 in. B&B); large transplants establish slowly.
Protect the root zone from grading and trenching — construction damage often shows years later.
Where oak wilt occurs, avoid pruning from spring through midsummer.

plants.nativeRange: Mountains and foothills of Arizona, New Mexico, west Texas and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Evergreen southwestern oak with stiff, glossy leaves and sweet acorns. A slow, tough shade tree for mid-elevation desert and grassland gardens.
designNotes: Drops most old leaves in spring as new growth flushes.
Prefers deep, infrequent watering; avoid lawn irrigation over the root zone.

plants.summary: Pyramidal oak with a straight central trunk and fine, deeply cut leaves. Tolerates poorly drained clay and seasonally wet soil better than most oaks.
designNotes: Lower branches droop; plan to limb up over walks, drives and lawns as it grows.
Becomes badly chlorotic in soils above about pH 6.5 — test before specifying.

plants.nativeRange: Southeastern and south-central U.S., north to New Jersey and southeastern New York
plants.summary: Fine-textured oak with narrow willow-like leaves; one of the most dependable large street and park trees in the Southeast. Small acorns and light litter.
designNotes: Transplants more easily than most oaks; tolerates heavy and wet soils.
Needs a large tree lawn — roots and trunk flare grow wide.

plants.summary: Fast-for-an-oak shade tree with a rounded crown and russet to red fall colour. More tolerant of urban conditions and transplanting than most oaks.
designNotes: Red oaks are highly susceptible to oak wilt; never prune or wound them in spring and early summer where the disease is present.
Needs acidic to neutral soil; chlorosis appears on alkaline sites.

plants.nativeRange: Southeastern Coastal Plain from Virginia to Florida and Texas
plants.summary: Iconic wide-spreading evergreen oak of the southern coast. Very wind-firm and salt-tolerant, it often grows far wider than tall.
designNotes: Allow at least 9 m from buildings; the canopy spread is the controlling dimension.
Sheds most leaves briefly in early spring as new ones emerge.
In the low desert it is planted as a shade tree but needs regular deep irrigation.

plants.summary: Low, mounding evergreen shrub with pink-white spring flowers and blue-black fruit. Common in coastal and desert foundation plantings.
designNotes: Entomosporium leaf spot is severe with overhead irrigation in humid regions; choose resistant cultivars.
Deer browse it heavily.

plants.summary: Large evergreen rhododendron with big trusses of lavender-purple flowers. Parent of many hardy hybrid rhododendrons used in northern gardens.
designNotes: Needs acidic, organic, well-drained soil; plant high in clay to avoid Phytophthora root rot.
Leaves curl in hard cold — normal, not damage.
Deadhead and prune right after flowering.

plants.summary: Low, spreading native sumac with aromatic leaves and orange-red fall colour. A durable shrubby groundcover for banks and hot, dry sites.
designNotes: Roots as branches touch the ground — knits slopes together.
Shear or mow every few years to renew.

plants.nativeRange: Chaparral of central Arizona, southern California and Baja California
plants.summary: Dense, rounded evergreen shrub with glossy, folded leaves, red buds opening to pale pink flowers in spring and sticky red fruit. A native informal screen for dry slopes that needs little water once established.
designNotes: Avoid frequent summer irrigation in heavy soil, which invites root rot.
Cold-hardy to about −9 °C; plants from Arizona chaparral seed sources are the hardier choice.
A sumac relative: some people react to the sap.

plants.summary: Disease-resistant, self-cleaning shrub rose that reblooms from late spring to frost without deadheading.
designNotes: Rose rosette disease (spread by mites) is common in the East: remove plants with witches'-broom red growth, roots and all.
Cut back by about half in late winter; do not plant long single-cultivar hedges.

plants.summary: Workhorse perennial with masses of golden daisies with dark centres from midsummer into fall. Spreads into broad drifts.
designNotes: Divide every 3–4 years to keep vigour.
Septoria leaf spot blackens lower leaves in wet summers; space for airflow.

plants.summary: Short-lived native wildflower that blooms its first year from seed and keeps itself going by reseeding. A staple of meadow mixes.
designNotes: Behaves as an annual or biennial; let some seedheads ripen.
Large-flowered "gloriosa daisy" strains are the same species.

plants.nativeRange: Mexico, the Caribbean and South America
plants.summary: Tough, fast-spreading perennial with purple petunia-like flowers. Seeds and rhizomes let it overrun wetlands; a Category I invasive in Florida.
designNotes: University-bred sterile dwarf selections exist; verify sterility before specifying in Florida.
Native alternatives: Stokes' aster, blue porterweed or wild petunia (Ruellia caroliniensis).

plants.nativeRange: Coastal Southeast from North Carolina to Florida
plants.summary: Native fan palm and the most wind- and salt-tolerant palm for the Southeast coast. Usually planted as field-dug specimens with a clear trunk.
designNotes: Field-dug palms arrive with fronds removed; leave new green fronds once established.
Very cold-hardy for a trunked palm, into the warmer parts of zone 8.

plants.nativeRange: Southeastern Coastal Plain from South Carolina to Florida and Texas, and tropical America
plants.summary: Airy native sage with spikes of tubular scarlet flowers from early summer to frost, one of the most reliable hummingbird plants for hot southern gardens. Short-lived, but reseeds into open soil.
designNotes: Grown as a reseeding annual north of zone 8; seed sown after frost blooms the same summer.
Cut back leggy plants by half in midsummer for a second flush.
Pink, white and coral selections exist.

plants.summary: Small woody sage with tubular flowers in red, pink, coral or white, blooming heavily in spring and fall. A hummingbird magnet in hot, dry beds.
designNotes: Shear by a third in late winter and lightly after the spring flush.
Needs sharp drainage, especially in humid regions.

plants.summary: Tall sage with cobalt-blue flowers held in black calyces from early summer to frost; a top hummingbird plant in the South.
designNotes: Spreads by tuberous roots; give it room.
Mulch the crown in zone 7.

plants.summary: Upright sage with deep violet flower spikes on near-black stems in early summer; reblooms when cut back.
designNotes: Cut spent spikes back to the leaves for a second flush.
Needs good drainage in winter.

plants.summary: Aromatic evergreen herb-shrub with needle-like leaves and blue winter-to-spring flowers. Upright forms make low hedges; trailing forms spill over walls.
designNotes: Root rot in heavy, wet soils — plant on raised or gravelly beds.
Some cultivars (e.g. 'Arp') are hardier, to zone 7.

plants.summary: Airy, silver-stemmed perennial with a haze of lavender-blue flowers from midsummer to fall. Thrives in heat, drought and alkaline soil.
designNotes: Cut back to 15–30 cm in spring as new growth appears.
Flops in shade or rich soil; compact cultivars (e.g. 'Little Spire') stay upright.

plants.summary: Upright native bunchgrass with blue-green summer blades that turn copper-orange in fall and hold colour all winter. The backbone of prairie and meadow plantings.
designNotes: Flops in rich or irrigated soil; upright cultivars (e.g. 'Standing Ovation') help.
Cut back in late winter.

plants.nativeRange: Coastal Plain of the Southeast, especially Florida
plants.summary: Shrubby native fan palm that spreads by creeping trunks into dense, long-lived colonies. Green and silver-blue forms are sold.
designNotes: Saw-toothed leaf stalks — keep back from walks.
Slow to establish and resents transplanting of large clumps; use container plants.

plants.nativeRange: Sonoran Desert of Arizona, California and Mexico
plants.summary: Dense, gray-green native shrub that makes a tidy natural or lightly clipped hedge with no supplemental water once established.
designNotes: Male and female plants; only females set nuts.
Frost-sensitive when young in colder low-desert sites.

plants.summary: Clump-forming goldenrod with arching sprays of yellow flowers in early fall — a major late-season pollinator plant.
designNotes: Goldenrod is insect-pollinated and is not a hay fever cause (that is ragweed).
Less aggressive than many wild goldenrods.

plants.nativeRange: Atlantic and Gulf coasts from eastern Canada to Florida and Texas; spreading inland along salted roads
plants.summary: Coastal goldenrod with thick, smooth leaves and large plumes of yellow flowers in fall, a key nectar source for migrating monarchs along the coast. Shrugs off salt spray, sand and road salt.
designNotes: Clump-forming and well behaved in lean soil; rich soil makes it tall and floppy.
Useful along drives and walks that are salted in winter.

plants.summary: Clump-forming goldenrod with dense, upright club-shaped spikes of bright yellow flowers in late summer and fall. Stays where it is planted, unlike the running goldenrods.
designNotes: Lean, well-drained soil keeps stems upright.
Goldenrod is insect-pollinated and is not a hay fever cause (that is ragweed).

plants.summary: Gray-leaved desert perennial with cup-shaped apricot-orange flowers in spring. Pink, red and white forms exist.
designNotes: Cut back by half after spring bloom to keep it compact.
Star-shaped leaf hairs can irritate skin and eyes — wear gloves.

plants.nativeRange: Central North America, with scattered eastern populations
plants.summary: Refined fountain of fine green blades that turns gold-orange in fall, with airy, oddly fragrant seed heads in late summer.
designNotes: Slow to establish; plant plugs closely for a quicker mass.
Long-lived and rarely needs division.

plants.nativeRange: Floodplains of Arizona, New Mexico, Texas and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Tall, vase-shaped native grass of desert floodplains, tolerant of alkaline and salty soils. Creates a bold seasonal screen.
designNotes: Cut back in late winter.
Thrives in basins and bioswales that receive runoff.

plants.nativeRange: Coastal Plain of the southeastern U.S., from the Carolinas to Florida and Louisiana
plants.summary: Southeastern native with large, fringed lavender-blue flowers over low rosettes from late spring into summer. Leaves stay green through mild winters.
designNotes: Needs moist soil in summer but good drainage in winter; crowns rot in soggy clay.
Deadhead to extend bloom; white, pink and yellow selections exist.

plants.summary: Late-season native aster with violet-purple daisies that fuel migrating monarchs and late bees.
designNotes: Pinch or cut back by half in early summer for shorter, sturdier plants; 'Purple Dome' is naturally compact.
Lower leaves brown by bloom time — face down with shorter plants.

plants.summary: Old-fashioned suckering shrub with intensely fragrant spring flower trusses. Needs cold winters to bloom well.
designNotes: Prune right after flowering; remove a few old stems each year to renew.
Powdery mildew is cosmetic by late summer; site in sun with air movement.
Blooms poorly in the Deep South and low desert.

plants.nativeRange: Southeastern Coastal Plain and Mississippi Valley
plants.summary: Deciduous conifer with feathery needles that turn russet before dropping. Grows in standing water yet tolerates ordinary and even dry urban soil.
designNotes: Forms "knees" only in wet sites; avoid next to mowed lawn edges if the soil stays saturated.
Hardy and successful as a street tree well north of its native range.
Wind-firm in hurricanes.

plants.nativeRange: Garden hybrid of English and Japanese yew
plants.summary: Dense, spreading yew for low hedges and foundation beds in sun or shade. Tolerates heavy shearing.
designNotes: All parts except the red aril flesh are highly toxic to people, pets and livestock.
Deer browse yews heavily; root rot in poorly drained soil.

plants.nativeRange: Southern Arizona, New Mexico and Texas to South America
plants.summary: Fast desert shrub with clusters of yellow trumpet flowers from spring to frost. Thrives in reflected heat where few shrubs bloom.
designNotes: Freezes back in hard frosts and resprouts; cut back in late winter.
Seed pods can be removed to extend flowering.

plants.nativeRange: Garden hybrid of Japanese and western red cedars
plants.summary: Fast, large hybrid arborvitae for tall privacy screens. More heat-tolerant and less browsed by deer than eastern arborvitae.
designNotes: Gets wide — space 1.5–2.5 m apart for a screen and keep 2 m from fences.
Replaces Leyland cypress in many screens where canker is a problem.

plants.nativeRange: Northeastern North America and the Great Lakes (species)
plants.summary: Narrow, dense arborvitae that holds a bright green colour through winter. Used for tight privacy hedges where width is limited.
designNotes: Deer browse arborvitae heavily in winter — protect with netting or choose another screen near woods.
Heavy snow splays the stems; tie or wrap leaders in snowy areas.
Needs consistent moisture; dries out and browns in hot, reflected sites.

plants.summary: Fragrant, flat-growing thyme that fills joints between stepping stones and takes light foot traffic.
designNotes: Needs sharp drainage; dies out in wet clay and humid shade.
Bees work the flowers — avoid in heavily used play lawns.

plants.summary: Woodland native with maple-shaped leaves and frothy white flower spikes in spring. Running forms knit into a groundcover.
designNotes: Needs organic, moist but well-drained soil.
Clumping cultivars stay put; the species spreads by stolons.
