plants.summary: Dense, glossy evergreen groundcover for sun or shade in the South. Handles heat, drought and slopes once established.
designNotes: Edge it twice a year — it climbs trunks and walls if allowed.
Rarely flowers in groundcover use.

plants.summary: Glossy evergreen twining vine with intensely fragrant white pinwheel flowers in spring. Used on fences, arbors and as a shrub-like groundcover.
designNotes: Afternoon shade in the low desert.
Needs wires or a trellis to start climbing.

plants.summary: Compact, hairy-trunked fan palm and one of the hardiest trunked palms. Brings a palm silhouette to the upper South and sheltered mid-Atlantic gardens.
designNotes: Prefers shelter from drying winter wind and afternoon sun in hot areas.
In zone 7 cold snaps, wrap the trunk and protect the bud.

plants.nativeRange: Eastern Canada, the northeastern U.S. and the Appalachians
plants.summary: Graceful, shade-tolerant native conifer with fine, soft needles. Shears well as a hedge or grows into a large woodland tree.
designNotes: Hemlock woolly adelgid infests hemlocks across most of the East; budget for monitoring and treatment or use alternatives.
Needs cool, moist, acidic soil; scorches in hot, windy, exposed sites.

plants.summary: Tough, fine-textured shade tree with exfoliating, mottled bark. Resistant to Dutch elm disease and tolerant of heat, drought, alkaline soil and compaction.
designNotes: Not the same as Siberian elm (U. pumila), which is weedy and brittle — check labels.
Holds leaves late; nearly evergreen in the low desert and Gulf Coast.

plants.summary: Native shrub with white bell flowers, summer blueberries and scarlet fall colour. As handsome in a border as in a fruit garden.
designNotes: Needs strongly acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5); lower pH with sulfur based on a soil test.
Plant two or more cultivars for better fruit set; net against birds if harvest matters.

plants.nativeRange: Mountains of southern Arizona and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Dense, dark green native evergreen for tall screens in the desert, where few native plants give year-round cover. Flat white flower clusters in late spring.
designNotes: Slow to establish; plant 15-gallon stock for faster screening.
Can be trained into a small multi-trunk tree.

plants.summary: Adaptable native shrub with flat white flower clusters, blue-black fruit for birds and red to purple fall colour. Good informal hedge or screen.
designNotes: Viburnum leaf beetle can defoliate it in the Northeast; prune out twigs with egg-laying scars in winter.
Plant two or more genetically different plants for better fruit set.

plants.nativeRange: Desert oases of southern California, western Arizona and Baja California
plants.summary: Stout fan palm native to desert springs, with a thick trunk and a skirt of dead fronds if left unpruned. Hardier than Mexican fan palm.
designNotes: Unpruned skirts harbour rodents and carry fire; trim dead fronds in low-desert landscapes.
Very heavy trunk — budget crane access for large specimens.

plants.summary: Very tall, slender fan palm that quickly outgrows the scale of most homes. Common along streets in the low desert and Florida.
designNotes: Frond pruning at height is costly; consider shorter palms for residential lots.
Seeds readily near irrigation and water features; listed as a Category II invasive in Florida.

plants.summary: Arching shrub with trumpet-shaped pink flowers in late spring visited by hummingbirds. Many compact and dark-leaved cultivars exist.
designNotes: Species plants get large; compact cultivars (1–1.5 m) suit most beds.
Prune after flowering; some cultivars rebloom lightly.

plants.summary: Compact native wisteria that blooms young, with short lavender clusters in late spring after the leaves emerge. Far less aggressive than Asian wisterias.
designNotes: Flowers on current-season growth; shorten long shoots in late winter and again in summer.
Still needs a sturdy arbor or trellis.

plants.summary: Heavy, woody twining vine with long fragrant lavender clusters in spring. Escapes into southeastern forests, where it smothers and topples trees.
designNotes: Use American wisteria (W. frutescens) instead.
Vines crush gutters and lattice; seeds are toxic.

plants.nativeRange: Chihuahuan and Sonoran Deserts of Arizona, New Mexico, Texas and Mexico
plants.summary: Branching native yucca with fine, fibrous leaves and tall stalks of white flowers in late spring. Classic grassland-desert silhouette.
designNotes: Pollinated only by yucca moths, which depend on it.
Slow — buy larger specimens from permitted salvage or nurseries.

plants.summary: Stemless native yucca with stiff, thread-edged leaves and 1.5–2 m stalks of white bells in early summer. Variegated forms are popular.
designNotes: Spreads slowly by offsets; old crowns die after flowering.
Hardy and long-lived well into the Northeast.

plants.nativeRange: Big Bend region of Texas and northern Mexico
plants.summary: Tree-like yucca with a single trunk topped by a dense sphere of fine blue leaves. A striking cold-hardy accent.
designNotes: Leave or trim the skirt of dead leaves; trimmed trunks look cleaner.
Specimens are sold by trunk height.

plants.summary: Early native carrot-family perennial with flat yellow umbels in late spring that feed short-tongued bees and flies. A host plant for black swallowtail caterpillars and a bridge between spring ephemerals and summer bloom.
designNotes: Short-lived but reseeds; let a few seedheads ripen to keep a colony going.
Expect swallowtail caterpillars to chew foliage — that is the point; plant enough to share.
